n: David flees to Nob, a town of priests near Jerusalem. Ahimelech the priest is nervous to see the king's famous warrior arriving alone.

f.g: A town of priests just north of Jerusalem where the tabernacle seems to have been after Shiloh.

n: David lies, claiming he is on a secret mission for the king and has arranged to meet his men elsewhere. This lie will have tragic consequences for the priests.

f.w: The king hath commanded me a business

n: David asks for five loaves of bread or whatever food is available.
The priest has only holy bread — the sacred bread from the tabernacle — but will give it if David's men have kept themselves ritually pure.

f.g: holy bread, set apart for God

f.w: kept themselves at least from women

n: David assures him that his men have kept themselves pure, as they always do on missions, so they are fit to eat it.

f.g: Probably their bodies, or their equipment and bags.

n: The priest gives David the showbread, removed from before the Lord when fresh bread replaced it. Jesus later cited this to teach that mercy and human need can outweigh ritual rules.

f.g: “Bread of the presence” — twelve loaves placed weekly on a table in the holy place.

n: The narrator notes that one of Saul's officials is there: Doeg the Edomite, Saul's chief herdsman, detained at the sanctuary for some religious reason. This detail sets up a tragedy.

f.g: held at the sanctuary, perhaps for a vow or purification

n: David asks for a weapon, claiming the king's urgent business made him leave without his sword.
The only weapon there is Goliath's sword, wrapped in cloth behind the ephod as a memorial. David says, “There is none like that; give it to me.”

f.g: Here the priestly garment used for inquiring of the Lord.

n: David flees in fear of Saul to Achish, king of the Philistine city of Gath — Goliath's hometown. It shows how desperate David has become.

f.g: The Psalm 34 heading calls him Abimelech, perhaps a royal title.

n: Achish's officials recognize David — the “king of the land” celebrated in the victory songs for killing thousands of Philistines.

f.w: Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands

n: David takes their words to heart and becomes very afraid of what Achish might do to him.

f.w: laid up these words in his heart
f.g: took them seriously, thought deeply about them

n: David pretends to be insane — scratching on the gate doors and letting saliva run down his beard. In the ancient world people often avoided harming those who seemed mad.

f.g: The headings of Psalms 34 and 56 connect these psalms with this moment.

n: Achish is fooled: this man is clearly crazy — why bring him to me?
With a hint of humor, Achish complains that he has enough madmen already. David escapes with his life.

f.w: Have I need of mad men
